oig2016launch.title: HealthCare.gov: Case Study of CMS Management of the Federal Marketplace (OEI-06-14-00350)
oig2016launch.author: HHS Office of Inspector General
oig2016launch.quote: On October 1, 2013, HealthCare.gov experienced 250,000 concurrent users, much greater than the planned capacity. Website outages began within 2 hours of launch, preventing many consumers from logging in and signing up for health insurance. In reporting to the public, the U.S. CTO attributed the problems to high volume, which was five times the number of simultaneous users anticipated.
supports: 250,000 concurrent users on 1 October 2013
the U.S. CTO put day-one volume at five times the number of simultaneous users anticipated
outages within 2 hours of launch

oig2016six.title: HealthCare.gov: Case Study of CMS Management of the Federal Marketplace (OEI-06-14-00350)
oig2016six.author: HHS Office of Inspector General
oig2016six.quote: In the end, only six consumers were able to submit an application and select a plan on the first day of the first open enrollment.
supports: six completed enrollments on day one

oig2016method.title: HealthCare.gov: Case Study of CMS Management of the Federal Marketplace (OEI-06-14-00350)

thousands of documents reviewed
report number OEI-06-14-00350

oig2016test.title: HealthCare.gov: Case Study of CMS Management of the Federal Marketplace (OEI-06-14-00350)
oig2016test.author: HHS Office of Inspector General
oig2016test.quote: Shortly before launch, CMS determined that the system had much lower capacity than anticipated and requested that the contractor double capacity in 3 days. On September 26, 2013, CMS technical officials visited CGI Federal offices to assess progress on the FFM build and conduct testing. They conducted limited performance testing and determined that the website capacity could support far fewer concurrent (simultaneous) users than planned.
supports: 26 September 2013 performance test at CGI Federal
capacity far below plan five days before launch

oig2016planes.title: HealthCare.gov: Case Study of CMS Management of the Federal Marketplace (OEI-06-14-00350)
oig2016planes.author: HHS Office of Inspector General
oig2016planes.quote: A Terremark manager reported in interviews that “The request was to double everything 72 hours from launch. We had done an extremely large build for months. We were pulling gear from all over the world, renting planes to get hardware here that was intended for other clients.” The request for a 72‑hour buildup was made on September 26 (4.5 days from launch) to allow for at least 1 day of testing.
supports: Terremark asked on 26 September 2013 for a 72-hour buildup doubling capacity
hardware pulled from other clients and flown in

oig2016eidm.title: HealthCare.gov: Case Study of CMS Management of the Federal Marketplace (OEI-06-14-00350)
oig2016eidm.author: HHS Office of Inspector General
oig2016eidm.quote: QSSI, the contractor responsible for developing the EIDM, reported later that they did not know that all visitors to the website would have to enter through the EIDM system and, therefore, underestimated the capacity needed. QSSI officials reported in interviews that they believed the anonymous shopper tool would enable individuals to view health plan information without creating an account, and that CMS's decision to postpone implementation of the tool contributed to the EIDM experiencing heavier than expected traffic. CMS officials later confirmed that the (poorly named) anonymous shopper tool would not have been truly “anonymous” and would have required individuals to create an account through the EIDM even if they only wanted to view plans.
supports: all visitors had to enter through the EIDM
QSSI underestimated EIDM capacity because it did not know that
QSSI believed the shelved 'anonymous shopper' tool would let consumers view plans without an account

gao15238recovery.quote: Specifically, among other things, it doubled the number of servers for systems supporting Healthcare.gov, added virtual machines for the Enterprise Identity Management and FFM systems, and replaced a virtual database with a high-capacity physical database for the Enterprise Identity Management system... unverified: The widely repeated figure that HealthCare.gov was sized for 50,000-60,000 concurrent users. The primary sources opened give only the ratio: the U.S. CTO said day-one volume was 'five times the number of simultaneous users anticipated' against 250,000 concurrent users. The explicit 50,000-60,000 target was not found in GAO-14-694, GAO-15-238 or OEI-06-14-00350.

The widely repeated claim that a pre-launch load test failed at roughly 1,100 concurrent users. OEI-06-14-00350 describes 'limited performance testing' on 26 September 2013 finding capacity 'far fewer concurrent (simultaneous) users than planned' but gives no number. The 1,100 figure traces to House Oversight releases of internal documents, which were not opened for this chapter.

The post-launch monthly capacity increase: GAO-14-694 says CMS obligated $1.5 million to increase capacity 'from 50 terabytes to 400 terabytes'; GAO-15-238 says 'going from 25 to 400 Terabytes of monthly capacity.' The two GAO reports disagree on the starting figure, so neither is used.
That the October 2013 'tech surge' directly founded the U.S. Digital Service and 18F. No primary source naming the causal link was opened.

The identities of the individuals behind the roles OEI-06-14-00350 anonymises (CMS Administrator, U.S. CTO, CMS technical official, the Terremark manager). The report names none of them in the passages used.

That postponing the “anonymous shopper” tool is what forced every visitor through the EIDM account gate. OEI-06-14-00350 reports this as QSSI's account and rebuts it in the next sentence: CMS officials later confirmed the tool “would not have been truly 'anonymous' and would have required individuals to create an account through the EIDM even if they only wanted to view plans.” The prose therefore states only what the source states directly — that all visitors had to enter through the EIDM, and that its contractor did not know that.

That high volume caused the launch failure. OEI-06-14-00350 records the U.S. CTO's public attribution of the problems to volume, then states the issues were “not caused solely by a higher number of visitors to the website but also by core problems in website performance.” The five-times ratio is used in the prose and deck as the CTO's figure, not as a finding.

Whether both December 2012 and June 2013 independent assessments found the missing hardware capacity requirement. GAO-15-238 attributes the three listed weaknesses to the two assessments collectively, not individually, so the prose says only that they flagged capacity planning.
